the Department of Transport. 1. In January, 1967, Mr. Arthur David Price, who had been appointed to College Militaire Royal, St. Jean, for a one year term in 1965 and whose appointment had been renewed for a further term ending on May 1, 1967, was given notice that his contract would not be renewed for a further term. It was explained to him that this action was being taken as he did not have a Ph.D. degree and was not working fast enough toward one.
Maxwell Cohen, Q.C., dean of law at McGill University, in his report as commissioner under the Inquiries Act, found that the reason given was not the main reason for the decision not to renew Mr. Price's contract although probably one of the motivating factors. The main reason for the decision was a feeling of discomfort among the college authorities arising from rumours and gossip concerning Mr. Price. Dean Cohen went on to find that, while a degree of maturity and
*3254

good sense in handling the matters was lacking by college authorities, they had not acted in bad faith and that their decision was based on desire to safeguard the reputation of the college. maintopic: GOVERNMENT WHEAT POLICY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
GOVERNMENT WHEAT POLICY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave, seconded by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Muir), to move the adjournment of this house under standing order 26 to discuss an urgent
November 27, 1968

Government Wheat Policy matter of public importance, namely the catastrophic failure of the government's wheat policy resulting in the imminent loss of 200 million bushels of damp grain through lack of drying facilities, a blow to the economy not only of western Canada but the nation as a whole; and the refusal of the government to undertake necessary measures to deal with the situation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOVERNMENT WHEAT POLICY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
please advise the Chair as to the urgency of this matter?

maintopic: GOVERNMENT WHEAT POLICY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, I will confine my remarks to the matter of urgency. I am not in the habit of bringing forward motions of this type, but the urgency of this matter is so obvious and the opportunity for dealing with it in the ordinary way so lacking, that I am compelled to deal with it in this way. The occasion for the motion lies in the situation outlined at some length in a statement yesterday by the chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. W. C. MacNamara, in Winnipeg.
Briefly, Mr. MacNamara stated that unless immediate action is taken our economy is threatened with the loss through spoilage of some 205 million bushels of wheat stored damp in the bins. In order to show that the matter is not only urgent but also important, I am going to quote a sentence or two from Mr. MacNamara's report:
Even with maximum use of terminal drying facilities the bulk of the tough and damp grain will have to be dried on farms.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
And again:
A survey shows that terminal driers, operating at full capacity during the next eight months, would be able to condition about 100 to 150 million bushels of the estimated more than 350 million bushels of tough and damn grain stored on farms.
To emphasize the urgency of this matter, Mr. Speaker, the farmers cannot visualize drying grain for a period of eight months, because if spoilage is going to occur it will take place next spring. Only the climatic conditions of western Canada during the next three or four months, with temperatures around freezing, will preserve the grain over the winter, but after eight months spoilage will have set in.
Even this survey is optimistic, Mr. Speaker, because the truth of the matter is that our total drying capacity in all terminal elevators both inland and at the three ports is only 12 million bushels a month. For anybody who

can add and subtract the implications of this statement are clear; and I am sure the Minister of Agriculture can at least add and subtract.
This means a threatened and serious loss of 200 million to 250 million bushels. The loss to the economy is in the neighbourhood of $300 million, a serious blow to western Canada and to Canada as a whole. This outlines the importance of the matter to the economy.
Dealing with urgency of debate, there is no opportunity under the rules to deal with this matter in the ordinary course of events. I will, however, make a suggestion. If the government will undertake to bring forward the agriculture estimates today, that will satisfy the need for dealing immediately and urgently with a situation which could be catastrophic. The reason the government must act is that farm drying facilities, even if utilized to the full, cannot possibly deal with more than some 50 million bushels a month. This means that a period of five months, drying at full capacity, would be required to save the grain. But within a few months the grain could well be beyond saving.
The only solution I see is for the government, through the wheat board, perhaps by using the provisions of P.F.R.A. or acreage payments, to undertake to provide drying machines to those farmers who do not have them and cannot afford them, in order that the drying out of on-farm grain may begin as soon as possible. This is the only way we can hope to save the major part of the grain.
Government action is required, and required now. That is why I bring this motion forward. There is no other opportunity to deal with it except by bringing forward the estimates immediately. What is required is an immediate statement of intention by the government, and immediate action to provide financing of grain drying equipment. With that assurance farmers could carry on. Without it, our economy will suffer another, perhaps disastrous, blow.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT WHEAT POLICY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want with all the emphasis I can command to support the motion having regard to the urgency of this situation. Some while ago I moved a similar motion asking that this house take time to debate the very serious, even desperate situation that was developing in western Canada. This motion was turned aside, and between then and now we have lost much time to examine and prepare for the very critical situation that exists.
November 27, 1968

In all honesty I would ask the house now to seize this opportunity to see what can be done to stave off really serious losses as a result of the condition of this grain. I know whereof I speak, because I have a dryer operating on my own farm saving grain that otherwise would have been a total loss. This situation will be repeated on farm after farm in western Canada. There are things that can be done and should be discussed in this house. Those here who are able to advance solutions and programs that might be useful should be given the opportunity to place them before the government.
The government should bring before us and offer to this house the opportunity to discuss the situation thoroughly and examine all facets and all courses of action that may be taken to use the resources of the commercial channels which are available, as well as the resources that the farmers themselves may have available.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT WHEAT POLICY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me to point out that we support the motion for study of the western farmers' very urgent problem.
However, frankly, we deplore the fact that, when we talk about an eastern agricultural policy, we do not get the necessary support in calling for justice for our own farmers. In the past, we have asked that grain elevators be built which would enable the transfer of feed grain from the west to the east; this would help the farmer, especially in winter, when boats cannot navigate and grain must come by rail, which of course makes it too expensive.
We support the motion and understand that there are problems in Canada. However, recently we too have asked that a solution be found to the unemployment and strike problems in the eastern townships; but we did not get the required support from the house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOVERNMENT WHEAT POLICY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order. If I may interrupt the honourable member, I should like to remind him that the debate on the matter under consideration is limited, since we have to determine whether or not there is urgency of debate. If the ruling of the Chair is favourable, the honourable member will then be able to discuss the subject matter of the motion to be moved subsequently.

speechtext:
I was coming to that, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

Order, please. Very serious arguments have been advanced by hon. members who have taken part in the debate. It is not an easy task for the Chair at any moment to reach a decision on standing order 26. I gather that the special committee on procedure has been giving very special consideration to changing the conditions under which that standing order operates, which would, I believe, have the effect of making it much easier for the Chair to reach a decision and to take into account the views advanced by hon. members in such circumstances.
Hon. members know that what we have to consider at this time is not at all the urgency of the matter. Although I do not come from the western provinces, I fully realize how important and urgent this matter is. I have been in the house every day, of course, since
November 27, 1968

Government Wheat Policy the beginning of this session and in the chair I have heard the questions asked from day to day by hon. members on both sides of the house representing western constituencies. I have seen similar questions on the order paper.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT WHEAT POLICY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The responsible ministers have not been here.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOVERNMENT WHEAT POLICY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
A motion under standing order 26 was made earlier by another hon. member. I believe that was more than a month ago. All this indicates clearly to me- and I am looking at the question from strictly a procedural standpoint; hon. members must bear that in mind-that the matter has been under consideration, that it is not a sudden emergency as is required by the rule but is obviously a continuing emergency. I wonder whether there is a point at which a continuing emergency becomes a sudden emergency. This is a philosophical decision which I hesitate to make at this time. But when a month ago a matter was considered extremely urgent, and when every day since then it has been considered extremely urgent, I doubt that today, by reason of the fact that a motion is made, I can reach the conclusion that it has now become a sudden emergency.
On the other hand, I have to take into account that there may be opportunities for debate of this urgent matter within the next few days. I hesitate to mention, but I believe it is my duty to do so, that there is always open to the opposition the possibility of moving an amendment to a supply motion, at which time this matter could be debated at length. This is a possibility which might be considered. After the exchange between the government house leader and the opposition house leader, I hesitate to suggest that they should get together-

maintopic: GOVERNMENT WHEAT POLICY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOVERNMENT WHEAT POLICY-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
-and perhaps try to arrange to set aside a supply day for a debate on this very urgent and important matter. In any event I feel bound by the standing order and by the rules and precedents inasmuch as they require that the matter brought before the house should be one of sudden emergency. This is primarily a matter of a continuing emergency. Because in my view it should be possible for the house within the next few days to arrange for that kind of debate, I would be inclined to refuse the motion. At the same time I advance the possibility that the motion might be brought forth again later if

there does not seem to be an improvement in the situation and if there does not appear to be the possibility within the next few days of a debate being provided with the agreement of hon. members from both sides of the house. Having said all this-and much of it might be not entirely relevant-I must reach the conclusion that I cannot accept the motion.

speechtext: Vote No. 1 will be found at page 392 of the blue book and the details are listed on page 394. For the information of hon. members these estimates were last considered on November 4 and 19.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak on item 1 of the public works estimates. I have long been interested in public works
November 27, 1968

and I have often been concerned about what has motivated the government in some of its actions in administering this vast department. For example, I note that each year for the last three years we spent $180,000 in improving wharves. We have also done some dredging for Canadian Vickers at Montreal. Canadian Vickers is a worthy industry. I ask the minister, why are some wharves and some drydocks improved while others are neglected?
Two years ago when I was in Vancouver with the agricultural committee I saw how dilapidated the dock facilities were. Recently the port at Vancouver has become one of our major ports through which goods are exported from Canada. Yet I found buildings there which were, as people say in western Canada, as old as the hills. The dredging going on in the harbour was 20 years behind the times. What most concerned me was the lack of an over-all plan for the building of larger facilities at that port to enable the movement of a greater volume of commodities.
Without doubt, the attention of western Canada is focused on Vancouver as a port of export. Hon. members no doubt are aware of the serious situation in western Canada at the terminals and in government elevators. I know that terminal elevators need not necessarily come under the Department of Public Works. Yet when talking about port facilities one must include terminal elevators, and in western Canada we have been worried for the past month because these elevators have not worked at full capacity. They work five days a week and less than 24 hours a day.
We all realize that if the government, and particularly the Department of Public Works, showed a greater interest in this matter they would bring about modernization of port facilities and facilitate the handling of Canadian products. Those products, of course, include grain coming from the terminals and from the dryers. Of course, many realize that one of our bottlenecks in grain has been in drying it. Dryers operate in the terminals. If grain has to be dried elevator companies sometimes do not know where to put it. They have no place to put it. Surely the solution of this problem has something to do with the Department of Public Works and the operations of the department with regard to improving harbour facilities, dredging, and facilitating the movement of Canadian products to export markets.
I could not bring myself to admit when I toured the port of Vancouver, and the Lake-head shortly after, that the facilities I saw
Supply-Public Works
were modern or that the dredging operations at Vancouver, particularly, were up to date. I could only conclude that we are behind the times. It was realized that Asia was a gigantic market and that we should streamline our port facilities to accommodate that market. But we were late. And we have had to pay the price for allowing our harbour facilities to fall behind.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
We hear a great deal nowadays from the Minister of Transport about the government's intention to build a brand new port on a sandy peninsula. The minister has not told us how he proposes to stop the sand drifting in without continual dredging. He has not told us whether the legal situation between the federal government and the province has been ironed out. With present pressure on the shipment of Canadian products, whether they be potash, iron ore or grain, surely there is urgent need to iron out the red tape and speed up the modernization of our port facilities and the development of new ones.
Looking over this year's estimates I find very little change in the total expenditure compared with last year. There is an increase of some $11 million. No real savings have been made in any of the items. There is really just a continuation of programs which have not proven to be particularly successful in the past. No consideration has apparently been given to the change which has taken place in the pattern of Canadian exports particularly from the Lakehead and the west coast. We see the United States taking advantage of our harbour facilities at Baie Comeau, for example, while we are failing to keep abreast of our leading export competitor. This should be brought sharply to the attention of the government.
One could go into the whole question of grain drying and grain drying facilities at these harbours. They have not proved good enough. A few years ago when the question of grain dryers on prairie farms was raised Mr. McNamara, chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, advised against farmers purchasing dryers on account of the danger of damaging the quality of Canadian wheat. Yet today, because of failure to handle the massive amounts of damp grain on the prairies, Mr. McNamara is urging farmers to get into the business of drying their own grain. He has thrown his caution of a few years ago to the winds and has said in effect: Get into the business because the government cannot handle the 380 million bushels of

November 27, 1968
Supply-Public Works
damp, tough grain which will have to be dried this winter.
The picture is plain to see. Certainly we must improve the dredging oi our major ports. We must improve the buildings, the basic installations necessary for the handling of Canadian products. It is necessary to streamline port facilities. It is not good enough to put up modern buildings here and there while the railroad leading to them is tied up by city traffic for half a day before the cars can get in there. We remember the situation two years ago when box cars were piled up from Vancouver almost to the rockies because of the difficulty of moving cars to the terminals. The fact is that the activities of the Department of Public Works, the Department of Transport and the Board of Grain Commissioners which handles the terminal elevators, must all be dovetailed together. In other words, one department has to know what the other is doing; they have to work together if we are to keep abreast of the demand nationally and internationally for Canadian products.
I can only say once again this fall that we in Canada have failed to keep abreast of the need for improved harbour facilities, particularly to deal with damp grain, a problem which is causing severe hardship to many prairie farmers because in consequence they have not been able to market their grain. They face the situation that if the grain is not marketed before early spring there will be a tremendous amount of spoilage and wastage. For this reason I urge the Department of Public Works to get together with the other departments concerned and not only give Canadian Vickers a subsidy of $180,000 every year but facilitate the marketing of Canadian goods and streamline the handling of Canadian products even if this includes the drying and cleaning of Canadian grain which has played such a major part in increasing Canada's exports during the past number of years.

Mr. Chairman, I, too, went on that trip two years ago when members of the agricultural committee learned a great deal about the agricultural problems of various areas of this country. I was impressed this afternoon by the motion which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain put forward with regard to western agriculture and I was surprised that members of the government did not take the opportunity to announce the changes which I am sure are necessary. When a motion of that kind is moved I am often impressed not so much by

the arguments as to the urgency of debate as by the indications that if a debate were allowed members of the house would be in a position to offer practical suggestions to solve the problems which had led to the demand for a debate. If the house is not capable of suggesting any solution to those problems then in my view there is really not much point in having a debate at all. But if a genuine crisis develops I am of the opinion that some consideration should be paid to the readiness of hon. members to offer their solutions.
I realize the minister is wondering what this has to do with the estimates of the Department of Public Works. I am coming to that. The department is responsible, among other things, for providing the facilities needed by the grain trade in western Canada. I was surprised that one very vociferous group, the wheat board, under the able leadership of its chairman, was able to provide itself with new facilities which were probably long overdue. I was equally surprised when an even more influential group, the Board of Grain Commissioners, failed to obtain new facilities. The minister may say he will not build them but I suggest he should be interested in extending the influence of the Department of Public Works into the construction of all public developments in Canada.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
When I visited the Moose Jaw terminal, one of the large inland terminals discussed today by a number of hon. members when they spoke about the drying of grain, I was surprised to discover it was built 50 or 60 years ago and very little change has been made in it since. In fact the method of dumping grain there has hardly changed at all from the time wagons were used right through to the use of rail cars. This is another matter that must be considered. Most of the box cars still use the side dumping method, archaic beyond imagination in the context of a commodity which is one of the largest revenue producers for a great portion of our nation.
Damp grain is a serious problem at present, and if the government considers the construction of drying facilities this would likely come under the responsibility of the Minister of Public Works. The fact that there are no additional drying facilities at Moose Jaw indicates that the government has failed to meet a need it should have foreseen. Over the years farmers have been plagued with cyclical problems of drought and damp grain, and had the motion been allowed for a debate
November 27, 1968

today I would have suggested the construction of permanent drying facilities at the inland terminals. Grain could be transported to them for drying and rerouted to country elevators for storage. Although this would not be the best way to handle grain it would be better than putting damp grain into country elevators where, as a result of weather conditions, it may become a partial or total loss.
One of the recurring problems has been the shortage of box cars at the harbour and inland terminals. On occasion this has been due to the reluctance of the Canadian Pacific Railway to provide box cars at terminals when it was more advantageous for the railway to use them elsewhere. I know this is not the responsibility of the minister, but I think he will agree that if he provides additional drying facilities at the inland terminals and damp grain cannot be delivered there because of a shortage of box cars, the whole process will break down.
On a number of occasions we have appointed a transportation commissioner and given him control over box car allocation. This is something that should be considered in the present situation. Such a commissioner could allocate box cars to areas from which it is necessary to move damp grain.
We have spent years and much effort developing markets throughout the world for our grain. We are not going to be able to sell damp grain on the export market. No one in eastern Canada will be interested in buying feed grain if the present situation is not rectified.
I have visited the terminal elevators on the west coast and at the Lakehead elevator complex and have been surprised that the construction we have undertaken is not meeting the ordinary needs of today. Recently I read a pamphlet issued by the Japan trade centre dealing with a complete change in the type of shipping that will be used to handle many types of cargoes. Many new ships are being built to carry container cargoes. The containers measure 8 feet by 8 feet by 20 feet and 700 or 800 of them are carried on one ship. It is possible that we shall soon be exploring this method of moving grain from our inland terminals and, if so, the facilities at those terminals will have to be changed accordingly.
All of us remember the efforts made by the hon. member for Skeena to have port and grain handling facilities expanded at Prince Rupert. His efforts were opposed both by the hon. member for Calgary Centre and the hon.
Supply-Public Works
member for Niagara Falls when they occupied the position of minister of agriculture. However, I know that the Minister of Public Works, who comes from Canada's western maritime province, is familiar with the development taking place at Prince Rupert and knows the role played by the hon. member for Skeena in that development. The changes made at Prince Rupert will result in that port being able to handle new methods of cargo transportation.
If the government would direct the Department of Public Works to undertake new construction at inland terminals I believe that department has the necessary planning and construction know-how, although these things have not always been evident as some of my friends will argue in the case of the National Arts Centre in Ottawa. I am sure the minister will also agree that if his department rather than Mr. Bennett had had some say in the development of the facilities to be provided in the Roberts Bank project things would have been handled in a much more advantageous manner and many of the problems developing in the area might have been avoided. It is my opinion the minister has the facility to foresee some of the construction needs in his own area. Had he done so he might have avoided the problems which are now developing in western Canada, particularly those in respect of the lamentable situation which gave cause for an hon. member to stand up this afternoon and say we are not only drying a very limited amount of grain in terminal elevators but in inland elevators as well.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The members of the committee made a study of this situation and recommended that construction be undertaken to modernize the facilities for drying grain at a number of points on the prairies. As far as I know this has not been followed up by any concrete action. I presume that the drying facilities at the inland elevators have not been improved and that in fact there has been no substantial gain.
Those are the few remarks I wanted to make in this regard. I feel that the Department of Public Works has a responsibility in this field and that this house has the responsibility to pursue every avenue to see that a long term or permanent solution is found for some of these problems which occur year after year to plague various areas. One of these problems relates to inland terminals and is the result of the fact that we have not

November 27, 1968
Supply-Public Works
constructed new facilities or modernized those built many years ago to meet horse and buggy demands in order to meet the demands of this modern day and age in which we live.
It is generally agreed by all concerned that this is one of the situations which might have been brought to the attention of the minister had hon. members been allowed to take part in the debate sought in the motion earlier today. It is my suggestion that the departments of government should not be divorced from one another and that when responsibilities affect large segments of our economy and our natural resources departments should work together so that an improvement accomplished by one will result in an improvement in the others.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak during the debate today I should like to say that in general I have supported the stand taken by the Minister of Public Works on the Roberts Bank super port issue in British Columbia. The minister was extremely forthright and decisive initially with the provincial government on this matter but as of late I feel he has been discreetly quiet.
I should like to make a protest about the veil of secrecy that has been dropped over the whole matter of the Roberts Bank superport, both by the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Public Works. This matter is of the greatest consequence to the future planning of the lower mainland of British Columbia and is probably more important than any project in recent memory.
As recently as August 17 I wrote a letter to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport and W. A. C. Bennett, the premier of British Columbia, in which I said that in view of the extensive ramifications of this project for the future of the lower Fraser valley and the resulting controversy, would it not be pertinent at this time to examine the Canadian National alternative route along the south bank of the Fraser river, a route which, incidentally, is favoured by the lower mainland regional planning board. Further, it would seem logical for a publicly owned railway to serve a port facility at least partially financed by the federal government. It appeared to me at that time and it appears to me today that this whole scheme has proceeded with undue haste, unreasonable secrecy and insufficient regard for the views of those people who are going to be most affected by this project.
On September 24 I submitted a notice of motion for production of papers and it was only recently, over a month later, that the

government finally agreed to produce those papers. I hasten to point out that I have yet to receive any of the documents requested, but at least the government is on record as agreeing to produce them at some time.
I feel now as I have felt for some time that there is federal pussyfooting about this project and that the government has been less than frank with the house about the Roberts Bank negotiations and agreements. It is not to the advantage of anyone that this be allowed to persist.
The original proposal, under which the rail line to serve Roberts Bank was to go through the finest agricultural area in the lower mainland and finally proceed along the shoreline of Boundary bay, which incidentally is the last major recreational resource on the lower mainland for the purpose of public recreation and also as a wildlife refuge, created a huge public outcry. Premier Bennett recently bowed to this public outcry and after one of his famous second looks ordered a study to proceed under Mr. J. Broadbent, vice-president and general manager of the Great Eastern, a provincially owned railroad.
Mr. Broadbent's study and proposals have resulted in some alterations of the original proposal so far as the rail lines are concerned. However, while conducting his study, Mr. Broadbent neglected to consult the chief planning agency for that area, the lower mainland regional planning board which represents 28 lower mainland municipalities and is ultimately responsible for lower mainland regional planning. It seems ludicrous to me that the chief planning authority for the area should not even have been on the team to assist Mr. Broadbent in his study and recommendations.
The Broadbent proposal, as some members may recall, suggested that the existing Canadian National rail line be used from Clayburn to Fort Langley where it would then connect with British Columbia hydro links and finally the port, thus avoiding the rather tortuous and very costly route through the mountainous area of Matsqui, known as Mount Lehman and Bradner. The proposal also suggested that the rail line be removed some two miles from the beaches at Boundary bay to avoid very serious despoilation of the last warm water beach in the area. This seems to me to be a compromise, but it may be only part of the over-all concept. I am forced, because I have no documents, to make some guesses and assumptions. This government leaves me no alternative by denying me
November 27, 1968

access to the information I need to be deadly accurate.
Two British Columbia cabinet ministers, Hon. Ralph Loffmark and Hon. Frank Richter, had previously assured the lower mainland public that the original route was by far the most economic that could be chosen. Paradoxically, Mr. Broadbent's route is now being boosted as being the cheaper by some $7 million. What kind of hasty planning has our provincial government been up to when a $7 million anomaly of this kind can manifest itself in so short a time? It reminds me of the Ottawa arts centre estimate.
Mr. Broadbent's second stage of recommendations disturbs me possibly a little more. It foresees a new C.P.R. bridge at Albion to connect with Fort Langley, thus avoiding the use of the C.N. line. This seems to be directed toward the development of a rail loop which would give the provincial government owned railroad complete access into the lower mainland area, and anticipates a causeway over the arm of Burrard Inlet to the present P.G.E. lines. Apparently what has happened here is that the public has been asked to approve of a half-loaf set of rail links, which probably implies more than we have been led to believe up to this moment. I do not think that a rationalized rail system is necessarily a sinister thing, but I am afraid that once we have agreed to a portion of the line it is possible that a much larger system may be forthcoming.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I do not think any one link in a rail pattern should be considered in isolation. The general public is entitled to know what are the overall plans and effects. I believe that by keeping this whole matter under wraps the federal government has defaulted in its responsibility for Canadian federal interests and has allowed provincial interests, the B.C. Hydro and Power Authority and the Pacific Great Eastern Railway, to drive a rather bold bargain with the national railways throughout the lower mainland.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?
I would prefer, sir, that I be allowed to finish.

I was only going to suggest to my hon. friend, if I may, that while I would like to discuss all these matters in my position as a member of parliament from Vancouver and a minister 29180-207
Supply-Public Works
from British Columbia, I would be entirely out of order if I discussed them now. They fall entirely within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transport, whose estimates will be considered immediately after those of my department. Therefore I am certain my hon. friend will have to repeat everything he is now saying.

Mr. Chairman, I assure the minister that I would be most reluctant to repeat everything I have now said, and I know the minister would not want that. However, since the rail links are directly involved in the access to the superport, I suggest this question comes under the minister's department. I would be most happy if I were allowed to proceed with this question.
The federal government has been reproved once before because it neglected its duty to the people of Canada over matters concerning rail lines within a province. I cite the pertinent parts of the case of The Queen v. Board of Transport Commissioners before the Supreme Court of Canada, and later the Lus-car case. Referring to the Luscar case, the judge said:
There again the criterion of the jurisdiction is the fact that the operations are a part of the interprovincial system.
The question of jurisdiction before the supreme court was whether an Ontario government system for commuter trains using C.N.R. tracks came under the federal board. The court held:
The constitutional jurisdiction depends on the character of a particular service provided on that railway line. The fact that for some purposes the commuter service should be considered as a distinct service does not make it a distinct line of railway. From a physical point of view the commuter service trains are part of the over-all operations of the line over which they run.
The court has since reproved the board and the federal attorney general for not appearing to argue for their jurisdiction and held that the provincial system was subject to federal regulation. On the basis of this ruling the physical character of the Roberts Bank route is that it is the sole rail connection from interprovincial rail lines to a federal port. That it may incidentally carry local deliveries from Vancouver by B.C. Hydro trains does not change the principal purpose or character of that rail connection.
Perhaps it would be to the benefit of everyone if there were a rationalization of the whole lower mainland rail system into a recognizable rail authority for the area. There is a federal interest involved here. I think the

November 27, 1968
Supply-Public Works
federal government, since it is deeply concerned with the financing of the Roberts Bank port facilities, should be very interested in the composition of any authority or group which will control the rail access to this very important port and the Vancouver waterfront generally.
I would like now to quote from the British Columbia Gazette of September 26, 1968. My quotation is from the Canada-British Columbia Joint Development Act under which easement rights were negotiated between the province of British Columbia and the government of Canada. The pertinent part of the document is found at page 479 and reads as follows:
-hereunder has now been reached between representatives of the board and of Her Majesty in right of British Columbia (hereinafter referred to as the "Crown") with regard to the period May 17, 1968-December 31, 1969, it being expected that, prior to December 31, 1969, a permanent solution of the matter will have been reached in respect of all periods subsequent to that last mentioned date.
Paragraph No. 2 provides:
The easement rights granted by paragraph 1 above shall nevertheless terminate on December 31, 1969.
I suggest this is an extremely serious matter. We are spending millions of dollars on a federally financed port and the situation is that we have an agreement with the government of British Columbia that is good for one year only. In other words, it is a temporary agreement. It seems to me the federal government must be on guard so that it is not put into an intolerable position in bargaining with the premier of British Columbia. I note that the British Columbia Gazette to which I have referred has outlined this matter in some detail. However, what is missing alarms me very much. What happens after December 31, 1969, if Mr. Bennett decides to change the rules of the game? Will we have to carry the coal by helicopter down the rail line and across the then closed easement in order that it may reach the ships? Will the federal writ, which incidentally is to the low water mark, force the Minister of Public Works to roll up his pant legs and wade from the docks to the waterway? What appurtenances are part of this lease? Where will federal services be established for the storage of material and equipment? Where will the servicing be carried on? These are very serious questions and we must be careful how we deal with them.
We all recall that in 1961 the previous Conservative administration was invited to sit

down with Premier Bennett on the Columbia treaty and ended up like the oysters in "The Walrus and the Carpenter". The National Harbours Board is now a tenant with a one year lease on the access to Roberts Bank, and Mr. Bennett is the landlord. One can visualize the renewal of that lease after December 31, 1969, being one where the landlord can padlock the tenant and where the board is at the dubious mercy of Mr. Bennett. When Mr. Bennett invites you to dinner, you might be the main course. I feel there has been an extreme reluctance on the part of the government to table the documents-

I shall try to conclude as rapidly as I can, Mr. Chairman. As I was saying, I feel there has been a reluctance on the part of the government to table the necessary documents. This is because the government does not wish to face a test of federal constitutional authority and wishes to avoid a constitutional confrontation with the provincial government at this time.
The federal government is undergoing an extreme paralysis in asserting its authority and the result will be a mish-mash of port authorities all across Canada. In the example before us we have established a precedent in that a provincial government has been delegated, by default, powers that can be used against the federal interest in future disputes of this kind. I ask: Is the federal government concerned about this? I know the minister originally was concerned about it. If the government is no longer concerned about it, why not?

Federal railways are now being driven into agreements with provincial rail lines, and once the authority over these matters is frittered away or delegated it might be very difficult to get it back. In addition, the port terminal operators, which include the federal government, will in future be at the mercy of any provincial government in a position to exert considerable influence over the various costs of service to these ports. I think what is needed in this area to avoid future controversies of this kind is an over-all system, a rationalization initiated by a public authority so that the interests of everyone concerned are planned and considered.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I believe we are on the verge of making decisions that are going to affect the planning of the area I happen to represent and the areas adjacent to it for the next century, perhaps even longer. In my view the decision to go along with Mr. Broadbent's compromise solution pleases no one, including the national railways. The railways however, appear to be prepared to subordinate their own views and rights in order to ensure for themselves access to the superport at a later date. 1 think it is interesting that both the national railways seem to consider the establishment of the port at this time to be premature, if only because of their considerable financial investments on Burrard inlet in the Canadian Pacific Railway docks at Port Moody and the Canadian National Railways Neptune docks on the north shore.
Expediency is not a sufficient excuse for regional planning. The federal government, by its reluctance to act, is assisting Premier Bennett and defaulting on its responsibilities in this very important matter. If officials would be more open and forthright in explaining their position, most of us would feel much more comfortable.
Various municipalities have been concerned about this matter. Although some are prepared to endorse the present compromise on the grounds that it will provide more industrial development for their areas, I do not think this will happen, and even Mr. Broad-bent seems to support the suggestion that high speed commuter trains do not really add much to the municipality's ability to attract secondary industries.
People from the lower mainland planning board still feel that the kind of energy devoted to the development of the Broadbent compromise might have been better directed. They continue to favour the route which

would provide a communications corridor along the south shore of the Fraser river and avoid the problem of the beaches. Some of them even feel that a causeway would assist in the development of port facilities in the Ladner area of Delta municipality.
I should like to say Mr. Chairman, that I do not think we can stand idly by forever. We have to search for all kinds of information with regard to what on the surface appears to be a very erratic position that has been arrived at in haste and protected by silence. That is why on this side we have been pressing for about three months now to get the kind of information we need. We cannot reach any reasonable and sensible conclusions on the basis of the rather tight-lipped and terse comments from the government side of the house.
The province appears to regard the lower mainland regional planning board as being the equivalent of some small pressure group. This kind of attitude is only too prevalent in British Columbia. The province has recently placed a dredging reserve for gravel right in the middle of Boundary bay. One is moved to ask why the federal government has not placed a recreational reserve in the same area. This bay is situated on the very doorstep of a great metropolitan area whose population is due to double by the turn of the century.
Finally, it seems to me that exhibited here is a total lack of co-ordination between the federal and provincial jurisdictions. Roberts Bank was a provincial game reserve in 1947, as was Boundary bay, but in 1968 Boundary bay has become a gravel reserve. Everyone wants to know to what extent there is federal interest in this development. Has the federal government decided to abandon its interest? Do we have to wait until we are in a real mess before we act? We will need a Pacific development board like the board in the Atlantic provinces in order to prevent the area from suffering intense religional problems. How will we integrate federal interests with provincial interests. Must we wait until we have an entirely new organizational framework? I do not think it should be necessary to impose a structure like the Atlantic Development Board in order to have the region extreme cost when it can be prevented by intelligent foresight.
I think the reason we are heading for a mess is that we have lacked the kind of courage necessary to go in as a federal authority and make the decisions we need to make. We

Supply-Public Works
have been forced to accept a compromise which is unacceptable, but we are doing this all the time. What will happen to the old Boundary bay airport? This airport can be easily declared a surplus property at some future time, just as Jericho was, and an entirely new interest could take over. At the moment it is only being used as a wireless station, although civilian pilots and some commercial transport pilots would dearly love to use this facility. The national wildlife service might be interested too in seeing Boundary bay became a wildlife refuge station and sanctuary.
People in this area are becoming extremely alarmed about where these rail links are going to go. The people of Fort Langley, for instance, are very concerned about what the changed route will do their community. There will be a line running through the very fine farmland along the Salmon river, and there is a risk it will destroy a fine residential area in the community of Fort Langley. Why is it necessary to have this third railway?
I should like to conclude by saying that the reason we have been so determined in pushing this whole question is that provincial political control of the lower mainland railways and port facilities seems to be the main stake in the whole matter. If this is so, we can deal with it. If it is not so, that is another matter, but in any event we are entitled to know what the real objectives are. Surely we can avoid a constitutional confrontation with Premier Bennett. We must be sophisticated enough so that we can plan with the province and do this whole thing openly. It has been suggested that there has been a public hearing with various groups. What happened was that Premier Bennett called to his office various petitioners one by one. This is not a public hearing.
I hope there will be some resolution of this hassle and I hope we can avoid constitutional difficulties. However, I doubt it because I think we will be heading toward this sort of thing as long as we keep matters of extreme national and, incidentally, local concern under a hat. I realize I have been persistent to the point of boring the house, but I do not think this is important so long as something is accomplished.
Finally, I think it is time the federal government acted decisively to protect the public interest and gave us a definitive legal opinion on whether or not it has the authority to take charge of this whole project and bring it to a reasonable, long term and sensible solution.

Mr. Chairman, in commenting on the estimates of the Department of Public Works, I must pay tribute not only to the minister, but to his staff, which I have met on several occasions. Quite a few of my colleagues, I think, have met these officials, particularly in parliamentary committees. This team which, together with the minister, ensures the efficient administration of the department, is exceptionally competent and particularly convinced of the importance of its responsibilities towards the Canadian public. For example, I am among those who have admired the ease with which these officials answer the most complicated questions, which proves that they know their department thoroughly.
They deserve to be praised for that to offset criticism levelled at them. Of course, Mr. Chairman, when a service of that size is concerned, it is always possible-to use a very popular expression where I come from- to pick holes in something and find cracks in the shield when one must absolutely find fault with something. I think, however, that the department is well administered as a whole. Moreover, I think that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) showed exceptional courage when preparing his estimates by cutting them drastically to meet that financial situation and the wishes of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) who had asked his colleagues to set an example to the provincial and municipal governments. In fact, he asked them to be extremely moderate with regard to capital expenditures precisely to prevent crises as serious as those we deplore in some European countries, such as England and France.
When the session began, Mr. Chairman, I tried for a few weeks to keep tab more or less of the amounts asked in this house from the Department of Public Works and other departments for works which normally should have been carried out only by the Department of Public Works. They added up to approximately $2 billion. I must say that most of those requests dealt with works which normally could be justified but that, under the circumstances, could certainly not be undertaken without seriously endangering the financial and economic situation of Canada and dangerously straining the budget. I am sure that the minister had to show great courage for he must have been subjected to extreme pressure. When one considers an administration as important as the federal
November 27, 1968

government, one must take into consideration the representations made to the ministers, the subtlety with which they try to establish priorities, to give precedence to what is most urgent and to put of! till the morrow what can wait. But this is not the main part of my remarks this afternoon, Mr. Chairman.
I would like, during the discussion of the estimates, to deal with the National Arts Centre. Many criticisms have been made about this national monument built for the centennial of confederation. I had the advantage of sitting on the committee which heard the evidence given by the Secretary of State-responsible for the National Arts Centre-his whole staff, the directors of the centre, those responsible for the various committees that studied the plans progressively, the architects, some government advisers, as well as officials of the Department of Public Works.
We questioned them very closely on everything. I do not think that one detail escaped our questioning, and we even questioned them at least two or three times on the same matter. Some of my colleagues are past masters at questioning witnesses and pumping them. Furthermore, people say in some circles that there has been a scandal. Here is a monument, they say, which was supposed to cost about $18 million, at the outset, and later $29 million; now, according to experts, it will cost $46 million.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, the opposition could see in this a golden opportunity to say that there was a major scandal. However, in spite of repeated questions, and all the subterfuge they could resort to, those who were interested in finding a scandal, could not even find a trace of one. In fact, Mr. Chairman, we have proof today that this building costs $46 million and this is, in my opinion, the most significant fact.
If evidence of squandering or patronage could have been found or if some politicians had taken advantage of the situation to gain some personal benefits, I too would say: "There is a scandal", but such is not the case. Everything has been conscientiously checked, not only by one, two or three men, but by dozens of men and at least half a dozen control committees.
There was, for instance, the commission set-up to prepare the plans. There were the architects and engineers and even consulting engineers. Also, the officials of the Department of Public Works. And then, of course, Treasury Board. Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that makes a team of serious people, very
Supply-Public Works
much aware of their responsibilities. Then, how can we explain such differences in costs between the initial estimates which were around $18 or $19 million and the actual cost of $46 million? It is very simple for those who seek the truth.
First of all, they had thought about building on a given site which was changed for all kinds of reasons that would take too long to explain. Then, they chose another site, only to discover that the subsoil was of solid rock. Therefore, the cost immediately went up. Then, after the preliminary blueprints had been completed, they realized that a parking space for 900 cars was needed. In a rock foundation, the cost of this would reach a few million dollars. Then, they thought special sound-proofing was necessary. Everybody will understand, of course that if, during a concert, one can hear noises originating from the furnace and from the air conditioning, music lovers will not be happy, especially if they are perfectionists. Thus, many things which were judged essential in order to have a perfect public building were added as work progressed. The construction of a $20 million monument which would not have been perfect would not have given us any national pride. Now, since it is a unique monument which is built once in a century and there are so few throughout the world, it was surely impossible for those who drew up the plans to foresee those things.
I agree that, in an ordinary construction, some time is required to establish plans, specifications and costs, but in the present case, it was an exceptional and huge monument. It even belongs to a field where we have no experience in Canada. It is even something almost unique, if we compare that centre with other monuments throughout the world, because ours will be more modern.
The whole construction was performed with all the guarantees which I have just mentioned under the supervision of those various committees and with the approval of Treasury Board. I myself put the question bluntly to some of the witnesses. For instance, I asked the deputy minister of public works: "Can you tell me that the monument we have there is worth $46 million?" And he replied: "Yes, of course, what we have here is worth $46 million. The difference between the original estimates and the present cost, the true cost, is due to the additions that were made."
Certain things, for those who are not knowledgeable, are absolutely scandalous. At

November 27, 1968
Supply-Public Works
one point, the director told us: "The curtain of the large theatre will cost $72,000." Mr. Chairman, can you imagine the reaction of those who know nothing about the situation. As for me, my eyes popped out when I heard that the curtain would cost $72,000. But, when we were told what kind of a curtain it is that it was necessary to draw up plans and specifications-when we were told that only one plant in the whole world could make curtains of that size and that it is located in Japan, I understood better. It is a plant which has been in existence for 800 years. Naturally, this curtain had to be packed in a special way in order to send it to Canada. One can then understand this figure of $72,000. It may seem excessive, for example, to people who have no experience of these matters, who live in isolated parts of the country and who are struggling with poverty. However, in the case of a monument which reflects the soul of a nation, this sum is not excessive, for the best is not too good for a country such as Canada.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, when a country reaches maturity and wants to compare itself with others, it must be able to do so favourably, and the best is not a luxury in our country. The National Arts Centre will be a source of pride for all Canadians.
Hear, hear.

It has been said that the way those things added up is questionable. Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that normally things are not done that way. It might happen that a construction project, even an important one, might include one, two or three additional features, but not as many as in this case. It is obvious. Monuments like that one are not erected every year; one is built every hundred years and it might be another three hundred years before another one is built. It is important that those additional expenditures be checked as they occur, that they be justified by various bodies that controlled one another.
This criticism was also heard: It will not be an economic proposition. Of course, it will not be so fundamentally. No one ever thought, for instance, that parliament would be a paying proposition in itself. That is obvious. No one ever thought that the C.B.C., set up as a public service, would make money.

Many other things are not economic in our country, Mr. Chairman, but if they are not, as far as money is concerned, they nevertheless constitute an enrichment for a country like Canada. Canada must provide Canadians not only with bread but also with culture and arts. Canada must give all its children the possibility of making the most of their talents and developing them here instead of having to go into exile to the United States or European countries.
So, Mr. Chairman, these things cannot be valued in dollars; they have an intrinsic value. These are intangible things that depend on money but which intelligent people understand; those who do not understand are lacking in intelligence and goodwill, or they are over-critical. That seems quite obvious to everyone. We say: It is a great luxury. But, after visiting the establishment and examining the plans, we realize that the building is really functional. Everything that we could describe as a great luxury does not exist. As a matter of fact, lines are simple, and costly accessories as we find in European institutions have been avoided to achieve a solid work that will perfectly meet the needs of the most demanding artists and even the perfectionists.
There have been insinuations for a time that Ottawa had been favoured to the detriment of other small towns that do not have the same advantages. That is a lot of childishness, stuff and nonsense, because Ottawa after all is the capital of Canada.
If we wanted to erect a monument which was to be the property of Canadians, then the right place to do it was in the national capital. Canadians and people from abroad, who will come to visit our jiational capital, will be very happy indeed to see the monument commemorating the first centenary of confederation. As for us, we shall have a little more pride in ourselves.
Mr. Chairman, some people have suggested that this building entailed extravagant expenditures. But figures never tell the whole story. We could have built a $20 million monument which could have been inadequate. This would have been wasteful expenditures and could rightly be called scandalous. Now, we have a $46 million monument which financially cost us more, but which meets all the requirements of the greatest perfectionist in the world. We can invite the most demanding companies of the whole world and they will be happy-and this is already evident-to perform here.
November 27, 1968

Mr. Chairman, we owed such a monument to Canada, our country. We owed it also to the young Canadians who will come after us and who will find here not only a reason to be proud of their country but also a place where they will be able to reach their ideal and continue to improve their knowledge in their field of interest. It will also be a centre to which our Canadian artists in exile will be able to return. Already a number of them are ready to come back in order to pursue their artistic career, thanks to the monument erected by the Canadian government which will be, as I say, a source of inspiration for all Canadians.
I think that it would be mean to keep on criticizing the National Arts Centre. Everyone readily understands what I mean. Therefore, we should try to make everyone realize that a country which aspires to such great fortunes, which is on the point of coming to maturity, and wants to play a part among the great nations, must from time to time achieve great things such as the National Arts Centre. Great things, of course, cost money because one does not get anything for nothing and it is not always the cheapest things which are the best.
In my opinion, it was a good idea to clarify the matter because it has been attempted too often to seek in that cause for scandal. Efforts were even made at a certain time to call the former minister of public works (Mr. Mcll-raith) to account, when everything had already been accounted for by a lot of people involved in every phase of the construction of that building. I call on the members who have not visited this Canadian Arts Centre to go and visit it as soon as possible for their enlightenment.

If he wishes to deal with public buildings in a general sense, then he is, of course, in order.

Mr. Chairman, you are right. However, allow me to point out very respectfully that in the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts, when questions were put to the Secretary of State about the construction cost of that building, he referred us to the Department of Public Works. He told us that if we wanted to deal with cost, amended plans, increases or extensions, we should apply to the Department of Public Works. Complaints were made to the Minister of Public Works, Mr. Chairman, and not to the Secretary of State.
I am speaking, of course, of the building which was constructed by the Department of Public Works and of its cost to Canada. In order to justify that cost, of course, I am speaking of the future use of that building. I apologize, because I seem to disagree with you, Mr. Chairman, but I think that it is not so much a difference of opinions. I feel that you were impressed yourself by all the good things I said about the future use of the building and I am pleased to have been eloquent enough to convince you. I hope I can also convince all my colleagues. However, basically my argument was meant to prove that the cost is not excessive, that the successive increases are largely justified, and that all the experts agree in saying that the monument, which has been added to in the course of its construction, is really worth what it costs us.
Besides, there may be a reason to justify why we proceeded differently in this case. Indeed, there was a date line. It had been hoped that it would be completed for the centennial year, which was impossible. So, Mr. Chairman, under the circumstances, there is nothing to fuss about. It is a beautiful monument and we should be proud of it. It cost no more than it normally should have.
I shall conclude on a short remark which has absolutely nothing to do with the Arts Centre but which concerns the Department of Public Works. I am thinking of the retaining walls along the shores of the St. Lawrence in my riding and in some of the others. In fact, I mean my riding and the neighbouring one. The Department of Public Works is responsible for the construction of those walls to prevent land erosion.
I should like to ask the minister, his inspectors and his officials, to proceed with this work as extensively as possible.
I have seen with my own eyes certain lands being eroded to the extent where the shore

November 27, 1968
Supply-Public Works
has now reached the house or the cottage. The tide or the waves have nibbled away, in certain cases, some 100 or 150 feet of land; trees measuring 15 or 18 inches in diameter have been uprooted. And some experts say: We are not to blame, the waves cause that.
I have had the opportunity perhaps a hundred times, of seeing that the erosion is caused by the waves, but, in most cases, by waves stirred up by ships that go by too fast. Year after year, those waves nibble away at the shores, to the detriment of the shore owners. I feel that very often the inspectors of the Department of Public Works are really too severe and blame too easily natural erosion for the disappearance of the land of the shore owners. I would therefore ask the minister whether it might not be possible to ask those inspectors to be, let us say, a bit more human in their conclusions or to file more complete observations and not to be merely content with spending let us say 20 minutes or half an hour on the site and then say it is erosion. Let them go and see at different intervals. Let them go there when large ships are going through. They will realize that, in my riding and in the two adjoining ones-and I speak of this because, naturally, the cottages there belong to people in my riding-navigation	produces erosion
which causes great damage and is very costly for the shore owners.
I think the same situation exists on the other side of the river; anyway, it does on my side. I myself have made representations to the department; in most cases, I did not get a satisfactory answer. Mr. Chairman, I intend to raise the matter again with more details because, in my opinion when these shore owners built houses 100 or 150 feet from the shore, they could not predict that their cottage would one day be swept away by the tide, which is more or less what is happening today.

Mr. Chairman, at this stage of the estimates I wish to ask the minister a few questions and at a later stage perhaps he may be able to answer them.
I say to my hon. friend who recently sat down that if he is worried about erosion problems he should consider the erosion that has taken place on the east coast during the last thousand years. He should thank his lucky little stars for his problems. If ships are giving his constituents problems the port of

Halifax will certainly welcome all those that go up the St. Lawrence.
Can the minister say whether his department is in a position to consider the recommendations of the so-called Murray Jones report that deals with the development of the general over-all land use within the confines of the port of Halifax and Bedford basin? Specifically, is the department able to make specific recommendations flowing naturally from the important observations contained in the Murray Jones report? On the Halifax side of the port I know the department is bringing to a fairly rapid conclusion the development of container facilities. It is appropriate at this time for me to ask the department to look at the long range implications of this development and to consider adequate and proper utilization of the land surrounding the basin and the port. In this connection the Murray Jones report is most important.
I apologize if the answer to my next question is a matter of public record. Has the government advised the province of Nova Scotia or the Halifax-Dartmouth bridge commission that it will participate in the construction of the second harbour crossing, the approaches to that crossing and the crossing of the northwest arm?
If I may be parochial, may I ask the minister to advise the committee of the present status of plans for a new federal building In the city of Dartmouth? Do current plans within the department call for the construction of such a building or is it contemplated that suitable and adequate space may be leased elsewhere?
My last two questions are of pressing concern to some of my constituents. First, may I make a direct representation on behalf of one of the more active fishing areas in the constituency of Dartmouth-Halifax East. I am speaking of Little Harbour, and the minister will know what I mean when I say I understand the department's difficulties with regard to Little Harbour. It is all a question of priorities. I urge the minister and the department to make provision for Little Harbour in next year's estimates. That, Mr. Chairman, is an unabashed and straightforward plea.
Finally, may I ask about the access road to an old and traditional area, the breakwater at Eastern Passage in Halifax county. The piece of land in front of the breakwater recently was sold for back taxes. The fishermen in the area had to acquire this land; they had to pay the back taxes in order to be assured of

access to the breakwater and the wharves adjacent to it. I respectfully ask the minister to look into this matter. I hope to ask the minister more questions when we come to later votes but for the time being that is all I wish to ask.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask the minister a few questions to satisfy my curiosity about an article that appeared in the Ottawa Journal on Tuesday, October 1, 1968. The headline reads, "DPW 'Philosophy' Switch Saving Taxpayers Money". The first two paragraphs of the article read as follows:
It cost something like $10,000,000-plus for the 18 floors of 220-foot high Judy's Tower out at Tunney's Pasture. And now public works is running up 23 floors of a new 253-foot high-rise two blocks away for $6,694,000. How come five more floors and 33 feet of height cost better than $3,306,000 less? And at today's construction prices, running far ahead of those of five years ago? The answer, says public works, is a "break-through" in a lot of things. But mostly in departmental thinking.
I wish to ask the minister a number of questions. Was a clear and precise building program formulated for the private commission as well as for the department's own design? On what basis is the public plan more economical compared with that of the private commission?
For example, let us take the over-all floor area and volume. What is the usable floor area and what is the ratio of net to gross. How flexible is the design? What are the respective finishes, exterior and interior? What is the extent of partitioning? Is it the same or will it be greatly reduced? What amount of built-ins and fixed furnishings is included in both cases? Also, what was the total environmental control that was required in both cases? What other features were sacrificed or felt to be unnecessary at this time? What would be the total cost per square foot of the building, if it were designed privately or publicly, at the stage when the building is ready for occupancy?

Are the hidden costs of public administration, such as use of office space, light, heat, janitorial services, building maintenance, depreciation, blueprinting, office supplies, general administration, owner's job supervision, etc., included in the comparison? Third, what assurance can be given that the new estimate will not be exceeded during actual construction?

When the Department of Public Works submits its publications for the people of Canada to read, this is the type of information which I think should be given.

Mr. Chairman, there are one or two constituency matters I should like to bring to the minister's attention. Some of them relate to wharves. First, I should like to point out that when the Columbia river treaty was signed and the Arrow dam built just north of Castlegar practically every wharf along the Arrow lakes was destroyed. Many of the communities had to be relocated. I do not know what kind of agreement the federal department has with B.C. Hydro for the replacement of these wharves but I suggest the minister should acquaint the committee with the terms of any agreement which may exist in this regard.
I point out that to date only one wfrarf has been replaced along the Arrow lakes. That wharf is at Nakusp. The department has done a reasonably good job; there are several complaints which I have taken up with the minister, and he is kindly looking into them. I am sure that quite often the hon. gentleman will find the B.C. Hydro authority coming to his department to say there is no need for the replacement of wharves at little places like Burton, Fauquier, Edgewood, or other communities which are springing up along the Arrow lakes. But they had these wharf facilities prior to the flooding. The new community of Fauquier has been in contact with me regarding the wharf; the people wanted to know to whom they should write. I gave them the minister's address and he may well have received a communication from them by now.
I suggest to the minister that in no circumstances should he allow his department to keep from these new communities which are springing up or which have been moved back from the water line the boating facilities which they enjoyed before the High Arrow project. I am sure it is only a matter of time before he receives requests from Burton and Edgewood in this regard, and I trust he will give them sympathetic attention.
The department has been dealing for some time with another wharf-really it is a breakwater and boat bay-being built by the town of Ainsworth on Kootenay lake. This is not a large community but there are not many communities like it in Canada displaying the co-operative spirit which this little community has shown. Public works engineers who have been there to see the boat bay and the breakwater estimate that at least $12,000 in
