labour has already been spent on it. They put a cat in to clear the area. They put a shovel in and dug out an area where boats could shelter. They hauled a vast amount of rock. They supplied logs and built a breakwater so that boats in that area could shelter in the event of a storm. The minister knows this lake well and he realizes this is the only spot between Kaslo and Balfour where a boat can run for shelter in the event of a storm. I have seen the estimates of the cost. They are fairly high; in fact, some local people believe they are too high. But I ask the minister this: will his department match the $12,000 in the coming budget? That is the least he could do, give an additional $12,000 to the people of Ainsworth so they can add to the structure they have started. Perhaps a further amount could be included in some future budget.
Let us give encouragement, for goodness sake, to a community which has the intestinal fortitude to go out and do something for itself. They are hoping to build a little launching ramp where boats coming from Nelson to Kaslo and Ainsworth can get down to the beautiful Kootenay lake, one of the best fishing lakes in Canada. We do not catch little fish there; we get them up to 30 pounds, big rainbow trout, and people come from all over North America to this fine fishing area. The local people need places to launch their boats. Today people have more leisure time than in the past. They have their little cabin cruisers and rowboats and motors and they need places from which to launch them. We need more of these facilities and I urge the minister to put this work on his agenda for the coming year. It is not asking very much when one considers the vast amount covered by these estimates.
There are one or two other matters I should like to deal with while I am on this subject. We have heard a great deal about roads to resources and there is one road in particular I should like to mention. I refer to the Stuart-Cassiar road. At one time the federal government used to share in the annual cost of this road. Cassiar, I might say, is a whole mountain of asbestos in the northern part of British Columbia, and the road is designed to give access to this area. I do not think a better expenditure could be made in this part of British Columbia than by completing this road into this part of the country and giving access to a region which is extremely high in minerals. Perhaps the minister could tell us why the agreement fell through. I know he has a difficult customer to

deal with at times in the premier of British Columbia. Sometimes the demands from the provincial government might seem a little high. But I do feel the federal government should be sharing at least in this particular road. The lack of money is delaying its completion. A lot of money has already been spent on this highway and I think we should continue it and make certain it is completed at a very early date.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I wish to say one more thing and it is in connection with Roberts Bank and the premier of British Columbia. I think two portfolios may be involved here, and possibly the Department of Transport is the one to which these remarks should be addressed. However, a number of years ago we had a minister here by the name of C. D. Howe who knew how to say no to Premier Bennett when the premier of British Columbia was wrong.
I recall when the deal to sell the water of the Columbia for a song to Kaiser was under consideration and how C. D. Howe told the premier of British Columbia, "We are not going to go for this foolish deal-period." The federal government of the day had the courage to pass legislation and stop the foolish sell-out of a resource.
We can erode federal responsibility to the point where it will become ineffective. I say it is now time for a minister in the federal government to stand up to Premier Bennett and say no. If harbours and national transportation are federal responsibilities, then let us have the courage to tell this man no and mean no.

of parliament. The individual member of parliament is given credit for obtaining those services which are part of the daily lives of the people in all areas as the result of the representations that he has made in the House of Commons. In other words, Mr. Chairman, this is a far more political department than the one I was in charge of formerly. However, I want to say to hon. members that in the operation of the department I will assure them that no constituent of theirs in any part of Canada is going to suffer for the sole reason that constituents themselves were foolish enough to put a member on the opposite side of the house instead of on this side. I think that is an assurance that is due to members' constituents in all parts of Canada. I give them it unconditionally, and I will see it works that way.
In this department we are dealing with a variety of extremely important services such as dredging, the building and maintenance of harbours, and the erosion of water frontage, the question raised by the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres. We are doing what we think is fair. Where the responsibility for erosion is at least 50 per cent because of the effect of transportation in rivers or the building of government installations, then we accept the full responsibility for preventing that erosion. Where it is less than that we try to negotiate on the basis of a breakdown, after discussion and investigation by our engineers.
Several hon. members discussed the important question of services and assistance for the tourist business. A very important tourist industry is developing for Canada through the use of pleasure craft. As a matter of fact my department has received a report from the west coast which shows that there are no less than 71,000 tourist boats in Georgia Strait. In passing I may say I have a friend who has a yacht in that general area, and he says that if we could only put the commercial fishermen out of business he could catch fish that would produce not 65 cents for a half pound but over $8 per pound. Indeed the tourist business today is extremely important and we have to pay more attention to it than we have in the past when we restricted our activities to dropping some stones to provide protection for pleasure craft. That is not the final answer.
I now wish to deal with the remarks of the hon. member for Western Nova who said that a number of fishing villages were inadequately taken care of in respect of accommodation. I draw his attention to the fact that we are
Supply-Public Works
moving into an era when larger boats are going farther off shore and, as a consequence, the type of facility required in respect of dredging and the building of docks is far more expensive than hitherto. Instead of building a great number of very small docks we shall have to point out to the fishermen that we will have to build a small number of larger docks which will require bigger expenditures. I would point out that in the case of representations which my department has received for the expenditure of $70,000 or $80,000 on a small wharf we have discovered that the amount of fish crossing such a wharf was not more than two tons a year. It is unreasonable on the part of people in such instances to expect that we make such expenditures.
I think it was the hon. member for Edmonton Centre who made reference to our intention to build utilitarian buildings. I am in favour of such buildings. I am of the opinion that a person who goes to work is entitled to a comfortable atmosphere but I do not think he should be provided with luxurious surroundings. He is supposed to enjoy that at home.
Tell Joe Greene that.

So far as I
am concerned, in the erection of buildings for the accommodation of servants of the public I am disposed to insist upon a greater degree of utilitarianism than in the past, and in the case of the building mentioned, which we are erecting for $6.5 million, about $16 per square foot, we are emphasizing the utilitarian nature of the building. At the same time I think the departmental buildings are entitled to have a little bit more sugar cake, if you want to put it that way, but when we double or treble the cost per foot in order to erect a building then I think we can do with less prestigiousness, and that is what we are driving for at the present time.
The hour is now six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and again I want to thank members who have participated in the debate. I want to assure them that in respect of all the questions they have asked they will individually receive a letter from the department giving them direct answers.
